note: See Introduction: Title; Author.

Third-person expressions in 1:2, 4 (“Let him kiss me ... The king has brought me”) open and close these verses, which are otherwise in the second person (“your love ... your name”); this shifting of persons is common in Hebrew and prominent in the Song. Note the sensuous nature of the language, which includes touch, taste, and smell.

verse_quote: your name is oil poured out.
note: The oil is the fragrant oil just mentioned, and having been poured out, would have filled the room with its aroma.

This is the first of five occurrences of the word “king” (1:4, 12; 3:9, 11; 7:5). Here in v. 4, there are two possibilities for the meaning: either the “king” is just that, a king, who has tried to win the young woman’s affections, or he is her lover, whom she romantically fantasizes to be her king. The latter interpretation is to be preferred (Introduction: Author).

**chambers.** The word “chambers” here as elsewhere refers to the bedroom, the most intimate of rooms.

**We will exult and rejoice in you.** We meet for the first time the female companions of the young woman. They are referred to as the “daughters of Jerusalem” (1:5), “daughters of Zion” (3:11), and “young women” (6:9). Here they serve to confirm the young woman’s appraisal of her beloved (see v. 2).

A self-description wherein the young woman expresses displeasure with her deeply tanned skin, perhaps because it makes her appear to be an ordinary laborer.

**1:5 tents of Kedar.** Bedouin tribes that live on the edge of the desert make their tents of dark goat hair, as was apparently the case with the tribe of Kedar. Kedar was seen as an exotic land (Jer. 2:10; 49:28).

**1:6 my own vineyard.** “Vineyard” occurs nine times in the Song, where it is an image of sexuality in general, as was the case in the ancient Near East, and the woman’s sexuality in particular (see 8:12).

The young woman provocatively inquires as to where she can meet the man at noon (v. 7); then the man indirectly but suggestively provides her direction.

**1:7 like one who veils herself.** “Veils” has the same negative connotations here as it does in Gen. 38:14, 15. The young woman does not want to be mistaken for a prostitute.

**1:8 most beautiful among women.** Elsewhere in the Song, this form of address is used only by the daughters of Jerusalem (5:9; 6:1).

The first descriptive admiration of the young woman by the man.

**1:9 a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.** Egyptian chariots were drawn by stallions. An ancient military strategy was to insert a mare into the mix in the hopes of distracting and confusing the stallions. The man uses the image to express his crazed passion for the young woman.

**1:10** **cheeks ... neck.** The first of many references to the beauty of the physical body. He begins by praising her in a modest manner.

In v. 4, the “daughters of Jerusalem” echo the young woman’s praise of her lover; here they respond similarly to his praise of her. The plural subject “we” goes against taking this verse as a speech of the young woman’s lover using courtly language, since “we” is consistently used by various groups at other points in the book (6:1, 13; 8:8).

The young woman’s lover is again presented as a king, as indicated by the following verse.

**on his couch.** Lit. “in his surroundings.” The surroundings may not be a literal couch but may refer to the outdoors (see, e.g., 1:16, 17; 6:2; 7:11–13).

A gum resin native to South Arabia; it is exotic and valuable. Mixed with olive oil, myrrh was used as an expensive perfume.

**between my breasts.** The sachet between the breasts is an image of intimacy.

Henna bushes produce a substance that is applied to the body as an ointment or perfume.

**Engedi.** This lush oasis is halfway down the western shore of the Dead Sea and contributes to the lush images of intimacy, and Engedi’s location between the hills mirrors the sachet between the breasts.

These verses express mutual admiration, as is clear from the repetition of “Behold, you are beautiful.”

**1:15 your eyes are doves.** Doves occur in the ancient Near East as a symbol of lovemaking or seduction. Here they evoke the young woman’s seductive power (see also 4:1). The young woman uses the same image in 5:12 (cf. also 6:9).
The Hb. word translated “green” means verdant, flourishing, or luxuriant, and it contributes to the lush images of intimacy.
The cedar and pine trees provide the privacy for intimacy that would be provided by a literal house.

The Hebrew indicates a plant of the bulb family, like a crocus or daffodil (text note). See Is. 35:1, 2.

**Sharon.** This plain extends south from Mount Carmel along the Mediterranean coast. Here the young woman modestly compares herself to familiar wildflowers.
In these verses, both the young man and the young woman praise each other as standouts among their peers., 3

Lit. “house of wine” (text note). The setting is outdoors (1:12 note). The lover’s “house” to this point has been the forest (1:16, 17). Now they move to a different “house,” namely, the young man’s vineyard, his “house” of wine. The expression continues the royal imagery from 1:4, 12 (the shepherd is a king) and the comparison of love and wine from 1:2.

**his banner.** An emblem typically used to mark out one tribe from another (Num. 2:3, 10, 18, 25). Banners were also used to muster troops for battle. It has been suggested that the word is used here for something like a sign for an inn. The young man is unabashedly advertising his love for the young woman.

Raisins or raisin cakes are associated elsewhere in the OT with religious rites, sometimes even in a pagan context (2 Sam. 6:19; Hos. 3:1), which has led some commentators to suppose that the Song originated as the script of a pagan fertility rite involving ritual sex (cf. Hos. 4:11–14). But the lovemaking in the Song has no obvious cultic dimension. The raisins here, like the apples, are simple aphrodisiacs. The young woman calls for raisins and apples to renew her vigor.
For the role of this verse in the structure of the book, see Introduction: Literary Features.

For comments on this refrain, see Introduction: Literary Features. Here the refrain is a reminder that the lovemaking should await the right time with the right person. The broader context of Scripture indicates that the right time is marriage, and the right person is one’s spouse.

The image of the shepherd lover as a gazelle or a young stag on the hills introduces and concludes these verses, which describe another outdoor rendezvous between the two lovers (see 8:14).

**2:8 leaping.** Reflects his joy and excitement to see her.

**over the mountains.** The mountains and hills are symbolic of the obstacles that must be surmounted so the lovers can be together.
Known for its speed and agility, the gazelle serves well as an image for the woman’s excitement as she longs for her lover to come to her.
Spring is a time of fertility, and thus the images of spring in these verses contribute to the picture of an intimate rendezvous.
The switch to the feminine form of the possessive pronoun “your” suggests that vv. 14, 15 should be assigned to the shepherd.

verse_quote: little foxes that spoil the vineyards.
note: The foxes are the one negative element in the otherwise idyllic spring setting of vv. 10–15, and they perhaps represent aggressive suitors who threaten the relationship of the young woman and her beloved. They could also represent her brothers. The imperative with no specific subject is like a passive (“May the foxes be caught”), and the whole verse is a wish by the lovers that nothing should be allowed to interfere with their lovemaking.
In view of the context, this is most likely a metaphor for lovemaking. See notes on 2:15; 6:2.

verse_quote: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee.
note: Traditionally, these lines have been taken with what follows, but they seem to make better sense when read with v. 16. The lovers have been together through the night, and when day breaks they must part. The young man’s return to the hills marks the end of the unit that opened in v. 8 (2:8–17 note). Alternatively, she may have declined his invitation to sexual love that is offered too soon.

This seek-and-find story has a more ominous counterpart in 5:2–8.

**3:1 On my bed by night I sought ... found him not.** The young woman is not with her lover but alone on her bed, and the verb “sought,” repeated twice, underscores her intense desire to be with him, while the fact that she “found him not” indicates at least some level of tension or frustration within her.

verse_quote: I will arise now ... I will seek.
note: The young woman is not passive but boldly takes the initiative to go out and find her lover.
The presence of watchmen patrolling the city streets indicates that it is night, and their role is more positive here than in 5:7.

verse_quote: I found him ... and would not let him go.
note:
The passionate search is over, he is in her arms, and she will not let him go.

**my mother’s house ... chamber.** Again the young woman takes the initiative, bringing her lover to the “chamber” of her mother, and since the young woman was conceived in this chamber, it is obviously a place of sexual intimacy.
This second occurrence of the refrain, like the first one (2:7), follows a scene of lovemaking and is another reminder that lovemaking should await the right time with the right person.

This is the fourth time that the young woman has pictured her lover as a king (1:4, 12; 2:4). These verses celebrate the joy of the regal wedding day (v. 11). Given that the Song is not a drama with a tight plot and that sexual intimacy has already taken place several times, we are not to interpret these verses as describing a wedding that is chronologically sequential to the previous material. Dischronologization (not ordering events chronologically) is common in both Hebrew prose and poetry.

Solomon’s men formed a bodyguard for protection from marauders, especially as weddings were celebrated at nightfall. But the verse has a double reference. There is also the “night” introduced in 3:1, which was spoiled by the young woman’s own “terror by night.” These fears are banished, at least for a time, by the splendid vision of Solomon with his fighting men.

An alternative name for Jerusalem (see 1:5 for “daughters of Jerusalem”).

**the crown.** This is not the king’s crown but the sort of garland worn by brides and grooms at ancient weddings. The custom was abandoned by Jews in their sorrow caused by the tragic war with Rome and the loss of Jerusalem (A.D. 70). A rabbinic proverb states that “a bridegroom resembles a king.”

**his mother.** The mother plays a prominent role in the Song (1:6; 3:4; 6:9; 8:1, 2, 5). There is no reference to a father, which is in keeping with what we find in other love poetry in the ancient Near East.

**the day of his wedding.** The real Solomon had many weddings (1 Kin. 11:3). The one day in view here may be a romantic ideal or a fond remembrance.

In these verses, the young man admires the beauty of the young woman (see “beautiful” in v. 1 and v. 7).

**4:1 beautiful ... beautiful.** The repetition indicates a superlative beauty.

**Your eyes are doves.** In the ancient Near East, doves were a symbol of lovemaking or seduction. Here they evoke the young woman’s seductive power (see also 1:15). The young woman uses the same image in 5:12.

**behind your veil.** The veil not only conceals but also reveals and thus intensifies the passion.

**Gilead.** A high plateau east of the Jordan River, compared for its beauty to the Lebanon mountains (Jer. 22:6; Zech. 10:10) and known as a place of fertility (Num. 32:1; Jer. 8:22; 46:11).

The location of this tower is unknown. It is not the present-day tower of David just inside the Jaffa gate of Jerusalem, since that tower is no older than the time of Herod the Great. The young woman’s neck is adorned with jewelry as the famous tower was adorned with shields.
The young man’s freedom to mention the young woman’s breasts shows the great intimacy of their relationship.

The time when the lovers must part is approaching (2:17 note).

**mountain of myrrh ... hill of frankincense.** Frankincense, like myrrh, was an imported aromatic spice (cf. Matt. 2:11). After the literal mention of the young woman’s breasts in v. 5, the “mountain” and “hill” could be a poetic reference to the same.

–**5:1** These verses (united by the sixfold use of “bride,” the underlying Hebrew word of which is used only here in the Song) begin with the young man imploring the young woman to come to him (v. 8) and end with their union (4:16b–5:1).

**4:8 Lebanon ... Amana ... Senir ... Hermon.** All these sites are in the remote north of Palestine. We are not meant to think of the young woman as living on the summit of Mount Hermon. Rather, the place names are symbols of the inaccessibility that the wooing is meant to overcome.

**my bride.** The word is used six times in this section (vv. 8, 9, 10, 11, 12; 5:1) and nowhere else in the Song, and thus serves to unite these verses.
In ancient Near Eastern languages, “sister” was commonly used by lovers as a term of endearment and affection. It expressed a closeness between people who were not members of the same family.
The compliment of 1:2 is returned, and it reflects reciprocity in love and affection.
These two terms are used together more than forty times in the OT, most commonly of the Land of Promise as great blessing.

verse_quote: A garden locked ... a spring locked.
note:
Images of the young woman’s sexuality and likely her virginity, both of which seem inaccessible to her beloved (v. 15).

**spring ... fountain.** Having mentioned her breasts (v. 5), the young man now makes poetic reference to the most intimate area of the young woman’s body.
The image of the enclosed garden is further developed (v. 12 note). In context, “shoots” seems to allude to the young woman’s thighs.

This image expresses that the young man would like his lover no longer to be a “garden locked” or “spring locked” (v. 12 and note). This is an implicit invitation to sexual union as the consummation of their marriage.

verse_quote: Let my beloved come to his garden.
note: The young woman unlocks her “garden” to her beloved bridegroom (v. 12 note). Consummation in the Song comes in the context of marriage.

The young man immediately accepts his beloved’s invitation.

**Eat ... drunk with love.** The speakers are not specified, but the ESV’s “Others” is in all likelihood correct. The chorus of young women joins in to celebrate the beauty of love.

These verses give a different perspective on love and sex than that found in the preceding verses. Here the focus is on risk and disappointment (see Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The final verse is the third repetition of the key structuring phrase “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem” and brings the third major section of the Song to a conclusion.

**5:2 I slept ... A sound.** Whether the young woman was deeply asleep and dreaming or sleeping lightly is less relevant than the fact that the sound of her beloved knocking awakened her.

**Open to me.** These verses are full of double entendre. “Open to me” is a request not only for entrance into the room but also for sexual union.
The young woman begins to contemplate the risk involved in opening herself to her beloved.
The young woman is aroused by her beloved’s actions.

verse_quote: I arose to open ... I opened.
note:
Having contemplated the risk involved in the relationship, the young woman decides to run the risk.

**5:5 liquid myrrh.** Myrrh in its virgin, liquid state, exactly as it flows from the tree, is a rare and precious substance (cf. Ex. 30:23). It is not clear from the Hebrew whether the girl has applied it liberally to herself before going to the door, or whether her lover has left it on the door latch as a token of his love. The repetition of the exact expression in v. 13 marginally favors the latter.

**5:6 but my beloved had turned and gone.** The young woman experiences deep disappointment rather than fulfillment. The Song is realistic in its portrayal of love and sex—sometimes delightful, sometimes disappointing.

**I sought him, but found him not.** Despite the disappointment, the young woman still desires her beloved. Her continuing desire results, however, more in frustration.
**they beat me.** Rather than describing physical abuse, these verses are better understood as describing the young woman’s mental and emotional pain.

This third occurrence of the refrain like the first two (2:7; 3:5) follows a scene of disappointment and frustration. This refrain is slightly different from the others in that it expresses the depth of desire the young woman has for her beloved despite her disappointment and frustration. Implicitly, it functions like the other refrains to teach the young women that love and sex should await the right time with the right person (i.e., with one’s spouse).

These verses are a sequel to the previous verses, as indicated by the repetition of language in 5:6 (“beloved” and “sought”) and 6:1 (“beloved” and “seek”). The young women want to join the young woman in the search for the young man.
Used of Esau (Gen. 25:25, 30) and David (1 Sam. 16:12; 17:42) as men of the outdoors.

The compliment of 1:15 and 4:1 is returned (1:15 note). The contrast with “locks ... black as a raven” in the previous line is striking. Her description suggests that her beloved displays both strength and gentleness.

**bathed in milk.** Probably refers to the whites of the eyes. The description of the eyes in this verse is an example of mixed metaphor.
Lit. “dripping flowing myrrh.” See note on v. 5.
The exact stone cannot be determined. In Ex. 28:20, the same type of stone is set in gold on the breastpiece worn by the high priest.
The relationship between man and woman in the Song is broader than lovemaking, although that is central to it. It involves companionship as well.
This language echoes 5:6 and shows the willingness of the women to aid the young woman in her search for the young man.
The young woman reveals that she knows where her lover has gone: “to his garden” where “he grazes among the lilies,” language used previously for sexual intimacy (2:16)., 3

These verses express admiration for the young woman by her beloved. Note how the boundaries are marked by the repetition of “banners,” a word that in the Song occurs only here and in 2:4.

**6:4 Tirzah.** This city, six miles (9.7 km) northeast of Shechem in central Palestine, is in a setting of great natural beauty. It was the capital of the breakaway northern kingdom for approximately fifty years after Solomon’s death. It continued to be a place of political intrigue until it was destroyed in the seventh century B.C. (1 Kin. 14:17; 15:21; 16:8–18; 2 Kin. 15:14–16). The positive reference to Tirzah here, particularly in parallel with Jerusalem, may support the traditional view that the Song originated in the time of Solomon, before hostility between the northern and southern tribes led to the division into two separate kingdoms, but see Introduction: Date and Occasion.
See note on 4:1.

The two references to queens and concubines indicate that vv. 8 and 9 belong together. In her beloved’s eyes, the girl is more beautiful than all the women of Solomon’s harem (8:11, 12 and notes).

**6:8 sixty ... eighty.** At its peak, Solomon’s har­em contained many more wives and concubines (1 Kin. 11:3), and there is already a suggestion of its future growth in the expression “virgins without number.”

**concubines.** A concubine was not an illicit or casual partner but a wife of secondary status (Gen. 25:6; 36:12; Judg. 20:4).

**6:9 My dove.** See note on 1:15.

**the only one of her mother.** The close relationship between the daughter and her mother is apparent throughout the book (3:11 note).

The young woman is praised here.

**dawn ... moon ... sun.** The young woman is described in language reminiscent of an ancient Near Eastern goddess.

**awesome as an army with banners.** The phrase is an exact repetition of the last line of v. 4. The praise given here is that of the girl’s beloved and concludes the unit (vv. 4–10).

These two verses are in all likelihood a short, independent poem in which the young woman recalls an experience of intimacy with her beloved.

**6:11** The word translated “orchard” is the feminine form of the same word elsewhere translated “garden” (e.g., 5:1). The orchard, like the garden, is a private place for intimacy.

**6:12** The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, but it seems to refer to the passion that the young woman excites in the young man.

The core of these verses (7:1–9a) is another instance of the young man’s admiration of the young woman. This core is surrounded by an introductory exchange between a group of men and the young man (6:13) and the young woman’s response to her beloved’s admiration (7:9b–10).

**6:13 Return.** The speakers are most likely male, as indicated by the response of the young woman, “Why should you [masculine plural] look ... ?” They are possibly the watchmen of 5:7 from whom the young woman presumably fled earlier.

**Shulammite.** The designation probably refers to the young woman’s hometown (Shunem) with a variant spelling of “Shunammite” (1 Kin. 1:3, 15; 2:17–22). The interchange of _l_ and _n_ in Semitic languages is well attested.

**two armies.** Or Mahanaim (text note). Mahanaim is the name of a town east of the Jordan River (Gen. 32:2). The nature of the “dance before two armies/Mahanaim” is unknown.
“Noble” here is the same word found in 6:12. There, the young woman speaks of herself as noble; here, her beloved speaks of her as such. In everyday life, she is a country maiden (1:5, 6).

This city east of the Jordan River opposite Jerusalem was captured by the Israelites in the time of Moses (Num. 21:25, 26). Excavations have revealed large reservoirs near the city, perhaps the pools mentioned here.

**gate of Bath-rabbim.** _Bath-rabbim_ (“daughter of many”) is probably the name of the gate, possibly one of the gates of Heshbon.

**tower of Lebanon.** The identity of this tower is not known. The great height suggested by “looks toward” or “looks over” Damascus has led some to take it as referring to the Lebanon mountains (cf. v. 5).

There are two places with this name in the OT. One is in the relatively arid south, in the hills west of the Dead Sea (1 Sam. 15:12). The other is the famous mountain where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal (1 Kin. 18), in the lush north. The latter is on the Mediterranean coast, due west of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), and is probably the Carmel in view here in this favorable comparison.

**a king.** The young man fancies himself a king enchanted by the beauty of his princess (v. 1; cf. 1:4, 12; 6:12).
Images of lovemaking (v. 7; cf. 5:1).
Here, similarly to 4:16, the woman responds to her beloved’s wooing with a willingness to yield to his overture.

–**13** In these verses, the woman takes the initiative and offers to give her love to her beloved.

**7:11 Come.** The young woman invites her beloved to the sexual encounter.

**fields.** The “fields” are once again the location of intimacy (6:2, 3).
The young woman yields not out of compulsion but out of will and desire.

The mandrake plant has purple flowers and an orange, tomato-like fruit, and residents of the ancient Near East believed it to be an aphrodisiac (Gen. 30:14–16).

**our doors are all choice fruits.** The doors are metaphorical for the meeting place of the lovers outdoors (v. 12). For a similar mixing of plants and architectural terms, see 1:17.

These verses express the intense desire of the young woman for her beloved.

**8:1like a brother.** The key word is “like.” She does not, of course, wish that her lover were actually her brother but only that she would have the freedom to kiss him in public and go with him anywhere without attracting comment.

See note on 3:4.

**she who used to teach me.** The daughter learned about marriage and its attendant joys from her mother, who taught her about the marriage covenant.

This verse is identical to 2:6 and precedes the last occurrence of the refrain (Introduction: Literary Features), which serves to remind the young women that the lovemaking should await the right time with the right person.

These verses continue the expression of the woman’s intense desire for her beloved, begun in vv. 1–4.

**8:5 Who is that coming up from the wilderness.** This clause is an exact repetition of 3:6, but there it is used in reference to the arrival of the young man. Here it is used in reference to the arrival of the young woman. The speakers may be the chorus of young women.

**leaning on her beloved.** This simple statement captures an intimate and typical pose of lovers.

**apple tree.** Presumably this does not refer to any particular apple tree but evokes the outdoor image associated with sexual intimacy throughout the book.

**I awakened you.** That is, “began to woo you” or, better, “aroused you.” The speaker is the young woman, and she is addressing her beloved.

**was in labor.** The verb translated “was in labor” could be translated “conceived.” The sequence would then be natural: aroused, conceived, bore. See Ps. 7:14, where this verb is translated “conceived” and is followed by “pregnant” and then “gives birth.” This is the only verse in the Song where the reproductive results of sex are in view; elsewhere, the focus is on physical (and emotional) pleasure.

A signet made of metal or stone and worn on a necklace over the heart or on an armband (Gen. 38:18).

**heart ... arm.** This pair signifies the entire person.

**strong as death.** Love is as strong as the most powerful, negative human experience. In vv. 6, 7, the emotional side of love comes to clear expression, whereas the emphasis throughout the book is on the physical side.

**jealousy.** In parallel with “love,” jealousy here is not a vice but a virtue that seeks to protect the relationship, like the jealousy of God (Ex. 20:5; Ezek. 39:25; John 2:17). Like God’s love, the love being celebrated tolerates no rivals.

The young woman has encountered numerous obstacles to love along the way (e.g., 2:8; 4:8), but her love has enabled her to surmount them all.

**wealth.** Wealth without love is of little value (Prov. 15:17; 19:22), and true love cannot be purchased.

An exchange between the young woman and her protective brothers.

**8:8 no breasts.** Probably not to be taken literally but to be read as a metaphor for the brothers’ perception of their sister as being too young for marriage.

**spoken for.** I.e., asked for as a prospective bride.
Metaphors for virginity and promiscuity. The brothers will honor the sister if she is a virgin but will rein her in if she is promiscuous.

The young woman allays the fears of her brothers by confirming her virginity.

**towers.** The young woman counters her brothers’ perception that she is too young for marriage. Rather than having “no breasts” (v. 8), her breasts are “like towers.”

**peace.** The Hb. _shalom_ here has the sense of well-being. By implication, the Song points to the marriage relationship as a place where such fulfillment is found. This points finally to Christ, for the ups and downs of marriage cause us to look for the one Spouse who fully satisfies our deepest need for love.

These verses, spoken by the young woman, are difficult, but the sense seems to be that her love cannot be purchased.

**8:11a vineyard at Baal-hamon.** Some interpreters have regarded this vineyard as a metaphor for Solomon’s harem, but the designation of a specific place suggests otherwise. The location of Baal-hamon is unknown, as is the reason for the reference, other than as a place of intimacy.

**for its fruit.** The keepers would pay Solomon a thousand pieces of silver for selling the fruit.

**8:12 My vineyard ... thousand.** “My vineyard” suggests that this verse is spoken by the woman. Here, as in 1:6, the literal use of “vineyard” is followed by a metaphorical use. The young woman’s “vineyard” is her body with its natural, rustic beauty. She is content to share her “vineyard” with the one she loves. Solomon can keep his wealth.

These verses conclude the book with one final articulation of mutual desire.

**8:13 you who dwell.** The Hebrew makes clear that “you who dwell” refers to the young woman.

**companions.** Perhaps the young women and the brothers.

**let me hear it.** The young man is eager to be alone with his beloved.

**8:14 Make haste, my beloved.** The desire is mutual. In language reminiscent of the lovemaking mentioned elsewhere in the book (2:8, 9; 4:6), the young woman invites her beloved to come with her.
